mainTopic: The wonder stories of רבה בר בר חנה: giant creatures on land and sea, the geese of עולם הבא, and the Arab guide in the desert
overview: This amud is אגדתא, a chain of amazing stories, not a legal debate. It finishes the story of the demon הורמין בר לילית, whose stunts on a stormy day ended when the king's house heard and killed him. Then רבה and רבה בר בר חנה report giant creatures they saw: a day-old antelope as big as הר תבור, and a huge frog swallowed by a snake that a raven then swallowed. רב פפא בר שמואל says he would not have believed the frog story if he had not been there. A series of sea stories follows. One fish wrecked and later helped rebuild sixty towns. Another fish was mistaken for an island. A third was so long that a fast ship took three days to pass it, and רב אשי names it a sea גילדנא. A bird stood in water so deep that an ax had been sinking for seven years, and רב אשי calls it the זיז שדי. In the desert, fat geese are waiting for ישראל in עולם הבא, and רבי אלעזר says ישראל will answer for their delay. After a סימן, an Arab guide who finds his way by smelling dust shows רבה בר בר חנה the מתי מדבר, and that story continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The end of the הורמין בר לילית story
steps.stepSummary: הורמין jumps between two mules standing on two bridges while pouring wine back and forth on a stormy day without spilling. The king's house hears of it and kills him.
steps.simpleTranslation: He stood on the two bridges of the river Rognag and jumped back and forth from one to the other. He held two cups of wine in his hands and poured from one to the other and back, and not one drop fell to the ground. That day was as stormy as the פסוק describes: 'They go up to the heavens, they go down to the depths.' This went on until the king's house heard about it, and they killed him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a story that started a few lines earlier, about the demon הורמין בר לילית and his amazing tricks. This is the final scene of that story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The stunt is meant to sound impossible: jumping between two mules on two bridges and pouring wine without a drop falling, all on a wild, stormy day. The story ends when word reaches the king's house (בי מלכותא) and they kill him.
steps.confusionAlert: This step starts in the middle of a sentence. The story began earlier, where two mules were saddled and standing on these two bridges. He is jumping from mule to mule.

phrases.english: on the two bridges of the river Rognag;
and he jumped from this one to that one and from that one to this one,
and he held two cups of wine in his hands,
and he poured from this one to that one and from that one to this one,
and not a single drop fell to the ground;

phrases.aramaic: וְאוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם ״יַעֲלוּ שָׁמַיִם יֵרְדוּ תְהוֹמוֹת״ הֲוָה.
phrases.english: and that day was a day of 'They go up to the heavens, they go down to the depths.'
phrases.notes: תהלים 107:26. He means it was a wild, stormy day.

phrases.english: Until the king's house heard about it, and they killed him.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the הורמין בר לילית story from the previous lines of the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A narrative report, not a legal ruling: הורמין's amazing stunt led to his death at the hands of the king's house.

steps.title: A day-old antelope as big as הר תבור
steps.stepSummary: רבה reports seeing a one-day-old antelope the size of הר תבור, with a huge neck and head, whose droppings blocked the ירדן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה said: I saw with my own eyes a one-day-old antelope that was as big as הר תבור. How big is הר תבור? Four פרסאות. Its neck was three פרסאות long, and the place where its head rested was a פרסה and a half. It let out droppings and blocked up the ירדן river.
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins. רבה describes a giant baby antelope he saw and gives its measurements.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא asks its own question ('How big is הר תבור?') so the reader gets a real number: four פרסאות. Then it adds the neck and head sizes, and ends with the droppings that blocked a whole river, to show how huge the animal was even on its first day.

keyTerms.meaning: An antelope or young wild animal
Parsa'os, a long distance measure (about four mil each)

phrases.english: רבה said: I myself saw

phrases.aramaic: אוּרְזִילָא בַּר יוֹמֵיהּ, דַּהֲוָה כְּהַר תָּבוֹר.
phrases.english: a one-day-old antelope that was as big as Mount Tabor.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַר תָּבוֹר כַּמָּה הָוֵי? אַרְבַּע פַּרְסֵי.
phrases.english: And how big is Mount Tabor? Four parsa'os.
And the length of its neck was three parsa'os,
and the resting place of its head was a parsa and a half.
It let out droppings and blocked up the Jordan.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new 'I saw it myself' report after the הורמין story ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A narrative report: a one-day-old antelope the size of הר תבור, whose droppings blocked the ירדן.

steps.title: A huge frog, a snake, a raven, and a strong tree
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה saw a frog as big as a fort of sixty houses. A snake swallowed it, a raven swallowed the snake, and the raven sat on a tree that held it up.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: I saw a frog as big as the fort of Hagronya. How big is that fort? Sixty houses. A snake came and swallowed the frog. A raven came and swallowed the snake, then flew up and sat in a tree. Come and see how strong that tree was!
steps.whatsHappening: Another giant-creature story. Each animal is bigger than the one before, and the point lands on the tree that could hold them all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story builds step by step: a huge frog, a snake big enough to swallow it, a raven big enough to swallow the snake. The punch line moves to the tree, which was strong enough to carry the raven and everything inside it.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: לְדִידִי חַזְיָא לִי
phrases.english: And רבה בר בר חנה said: I myself saw

phrases.aramaic: הָהִיא אַקְרוּקְתָּא, דְּהַוְיָא כִּי אַקְרָא דְהַגְרוּנְיָא.
phrases.english: a certain frog that was as big as the fort of Hagronya.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַקְרָא דְהַגְרוּנְיָא כַּמָּה הָוְיָא? שִׁתִּין בָּתֵּי.
phrases.english: And how big is the fort of Hagronya? Sixty houses.
A snake came and swallowed it.
A raven came and swallowed the snake,
and it went up and sat in a tree.

phrases.aramaic: תָּא חֲזִי כַּמָּה נְפִישׁ חֵילֵיהּ דְּאִילָנָא.
phrases.english: Come and see how great the strength of the tree was.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: לְדִידִי חַזְיָא לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another 'I saw it myself' report in the same series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A narrative report: a giant frog swallowed by a snake, the snake by a raven, and the tree held the raven.

steps.title: רב פפא בר שמואל: I would not have believed it
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא בר שמואל reacts to the frog story, saying that if he had not been there himself he would not have believed it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא בר שמואל said: If I had not been there, I would not have believed it.
steps.whatsHappening: A different speaker comments on the frog story he just heard. He says he was there and saw it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This line does not add a new event. It backs up the story with a second eyewitness, while openly admitting how hard it is to believe.

phrases.english: רב פפא בר שמואל said:

phrases.aramaic: אִי לָא הֲוַאי הָתָם, לָא הֵימַנִי.
phrases.english: If I had not been there, I would not have believed it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Comments on the frog story from step 3 and confirms it as an eyewitness.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An eyewitness confirmation: the frog story is true, even though it would be hard to believe without seeing it.

steps.title: The giant fish that wrecked and rebuilt sixty towns
steps.stepSummary: On a ship, רבה בר בר חנה saw a fish killed by a tiny mud-eating creature in its nose. It washed ashore, destroyed sixty towns, fed sixty more, and gave salted meat to sixty more. Its eye gave 300 jugs of oil, and a year later its bones were used to rebuild the towns.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: Once we were traveling on a ship, and we saw a fish with a small mud-eating creature sitting in its nostril. The water pushed the fish and threw it onto the shore. Sixty towns were destroyed by it, sixty towns ate from it, and sixty towns salted its meat. From one of its eyeballs they filled 300 jugs of oil. When we came back twelve months later, we saw people sawing beams from its bones, and they had started rebuilding those towns.
steps.whatsHappening: A new sea-travel story from רבה בר בר חנה about one enormous fish, from its death until a year later.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The fish is so huge that a tiny creature in its nose was enough to kill it, and its body crushed sixty towns when it landed. The same fish then helps people: food for sixty towns, preserved meat for sixty more, oil from one eye, and bones strong enough to be cut into building beams to rebuild what it destroyed.
steps.whatToRemember: This section is a chain of amazing eyewitness stories (mostly from רבה בר בר חנה). Each one shows how enormous these creatures were, and each is told as 'I saw it myself.'

phrases.english: And רבה בר בר חנה said:

phrases.aramaic: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה קָא אָזְלִינַן בִּסְפִינְתָּא,
phrases.english: Once we were traveling on a ship,
and we saw a certain fish
that had a mud-eater sitting in its nostril,
phrases.notes: A tiny creature crawled into its nose and killed it. The text assumes the fish died from this.

phrases.english: and the water pushed it and threw it onto the shore,
and sixty towns were destroyed by it.
And sixty towns ate from it,
and sixty towns salted meat from it,
and they filled, from one of its eyeballs,
three hundred jugs of oil.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי הֲדַרַן לְבָתַר תְּרֵיסַר יַרְחֵי שַׁתָּא,
phrases.english: And when we came back after the twelve months of the year,

phrases.aramaic: חֲזֵינַן דַּהֲוָה קָא מְנַסְּרִי מִגַּרְמֵיהּ מְטַלְּלָתָא,
phrases.english: we saw that they were sawing beams from its bones,
and they had set out to rebuild those towns.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה קָא אָזְלִינַן בִּסְפִינְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from 'I saw' reports on land to a sea-travel report in the same series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A narrative report: a giant fish killed by a tiny creature destroyed sixty towns, fed many more, and its bones later rebuilt the towns.

steps.title: The fish that looked like an island
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה tells how sailors cooked on a huge fish covered with sand and grass, thinking it was land. The fish flipped over when its back got hot.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once we were on a ship and saw a fish with sand on its back and grass growing on it. We thought it was dry land, so we climbed up and baked and cooked on it. When its back got hot, it flipped over. If the ship had not been close by, we would have drowned.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another sea story from רבה בר בר חנה, this time about a fish so big that people mistook it for an island.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This continues the chain of giant-creature stories from the earlier steps. The fish is so old and still that sand and grass have built up on it. The danger only shows itself when the fire wakes it up.

phrases.english: And Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:

phrases.aramaic: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה קָא אָזְלִינַן בִּסְפִינְתָּא,
phrases.english: Once we were traveling on a ship,
and we saw a certain fish
that had sand settled on its back
and grass had sprouted on it.
We thought it was dry land,
so we went up and baked and cooked on its back.
But when its back got hot, it turned over,
and if the ship had not been close by,
we would have drowned.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה קָא אָזְלִינַן בִּסְפִינְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Another sea story from רבה בר בר חנה, following the giant fish of step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fish so huge and still that sand and grass grew on it was mistaken for land.

steps.title: Three days sailing between a fish's fins
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה reports that his ship sailed for three days and nights from one fin of a fish to the other. The fish and the ship were moving in opposite directions.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once we were on a ship, and the ship sailed from one fin of a fish to its other fin for three days and three nights. The fish was going upstream and we were going downstream.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another story about a fish so long that a ship needed three full days to pass along it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The length is made even more striking because the two were moving toward each other, so they passed each other quickly. The next step answers the obvious objection that the ship might simply have been slow.

phrases.english: And Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:
Once we were traveling on a ship,
and the ship traveled
between one fin and the other fin of a fish
for three days and three nights,
it going upward and we going downward.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה אָזְלִינַן בִּסְפִינְתָּא, וּסְגַאי סְפִינְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new fish story in the same series.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A fish was so long that a ship sailing against its direction took three days to pass from fin to fin.

steps.title: How fast these ships really were
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא heads off the objection that the ship was slow. It quotes רב דימי that such a ship covers sixty parasangs in the time it takes to heat a kettle, and outruns a horseman's arrow.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you would say the ship does not move very fast: when רב דימי came, he said that in the time it takes to heat a kettle of water, it travels sixty parasangs. And if a horseman shoots an arrow, the ship gets ahead of it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא expects a doubt ('maybe the ship was just slow') and answers it with רב דימי's report on how fast these ships sail.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three-day trip only shows the fish's size if the ship was fast. רב דימי's figures, sixty parasangs in moments and faster than an arrow, make the fish enormously long. The objection and its answer come together in one step.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you would say (introduces a possible objection)
Parasangs, a long measure of distance

steps.confusionAlert: Nobody in the story actually asks this. 'וְכִי תֵּימָא' is the גמרא raising the doubt itself so it can answer it right away.

phrases.english: And if you would say:
the ship does not travel very fast,
when Rav Dimi came, he said:
in the time it takes to heat a kettle of water
it travels sixty parasangs,
and when a horseman shoots an arrow, it gets ahead of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכִי תֵּימָא: לָא מְסַגְּיָא סְפִינְתָּא טוּבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defends the story in step 7 against the idea that the ship was slow.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual support from a report (רב דימי)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The three days might only reflect a slow ship, not a huge fish.
steps.terutzMaskana: These ships are extremely fast, so the fish truly was immense.

steps.title: רב אשי names the fish
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the fish was a sea גילדנא, a fish that has two fins.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב אשי said: That fish was a sea גילדנא, which has two fins.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי adds information about the story in step 7 by telling us what kind of fish it was.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story spoke of 'fin to fin'. רב אשי identifies the creature as a known type of sea fish with two fins, which ties the story to a specific species.

keyTerms.meaning: A sea גילדנא, a kind of fish

phrases.english: And Rav Ashi said:
That was a sea gildana,
which has two fins.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: הָהוּא גִּילְדָּנָא דְיַמָּא הוּא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The fish was a sea גילדנא with two fins.

steps.title: The giant bird standing in bottomless water
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר בר חנה saw a bird standing in water up to its ankles with its head in the sky. When the sailors wanted to go down into the water, a בת קול warned them that the water was so deep that an ax dropped seven years earlier had not yet reached the bottom.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once we were on a ship and saw a bird standing in water up to its ankles, with its head in the sky. We thought the water was shallow and wanted to go down to cool off. A בת קול came out and said: Do not go down here. A carpenter's ax fell in here seven years ago and still has not reached the bottom.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells another story, about a bird so tall that water deep enough to swallow an ax for seven years came only up to its ankles.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The sailors judge the depth from the bird, and the judgment is wrong. The בת קול shows how gigantic the bird is by showing how deep the water really is.

phrases.english: And Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:
Once we were traveling on a ship,
and we saw a certain bird
standing in water up to its ankles,
with its head in the sky.
And we said: there is no water here,
phrases.notes: He means there is no deep water. If it reaches only the bird's ankles, it must be shallow.

phrases.english: and we wanted to go down to cool ourselves off;
and a Divine Voice came out and said to us:
Do not go down here,
for a carpenter's ax fell into it
seven years ago already,
and it has not yet reached the bottom.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה אָזְלִינַן בִּסְפִינְתָּא, וַחֲזֵינַן הָהוּא צִיפְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story in the same series, moving from fish to a bird.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A bird stood in water so deep that an ax had been sinking for seven years, yet the water reached only its ankles.

steps.title: Why the ax never reached the bottom
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא clarifies that the ax had not reached the bottom because the water was rushing, not because the water was so deep.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this was not because the water was so deep, but because the water was turbulent.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a short clarification to the bird story, explaining the real reason the ax kept sinking for seven years.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without this line we might think the water was deep enough to take seven years to fall through. The גמרא says the turbulent current kept tossing the ax around, which is what delayed it.

phrases.english: And this is not because the water is so much,
but because the water is turbulent.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָאו מִשּׁוּם דִּנְפִישִׁי מַיָּא, אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם דִּרְדִפִי מַיָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies the detail about the ax in step 10.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The ax's delay came from the rushing current, not from the depth of the water.

steps.title: רב אשי identifies the bird as זיז שדי
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says the giant bird is the זיז שדי mentioned in תהלים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: That bird is the זיז שדי, as it is written: 'and the זיז שדי is with Me.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי names the bird from the story and connects it to a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just as he named the fish in step 9, רב אשי now names the bird. He links it to the creature that the פסוק describes as belonging to ה׳.

keyTerms.meaning: The giant bird mentioned in תהלים

steps.whatToRemember: רב אשי ties two of the stories to known creatures: the fish is a sea גילדנא, and the bird is the זיז שדי of תהלים.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
And that bird is the ziz sadai,
as it is written: "And the ziz sadai is with Me."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: וְהָהוּא זִיז שָׂדַי הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Identifies the bird from step 10 using a פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The giant bird is the זיז שדי of תהלים.

steps.title: The fat geese in the desert
steps.stepSummary: In the desert, רבה בר בר חנה saw geese so fat that their wings drooped and oil flowed beneath them. He asked whether ישראל would have a share of them in עולם הבא, and they lifted a wing and a leg.
steps.simpleTranslation: Once we were traveling in the desert and saw geese so fat that their wings drooped, and streams of oil flowed from under them. I asked them: Will we have a share of you in עולם הבא? One lifted a wing, and one lifted a leg.
steps.whatsHappening: The scene moves from the sea to the desert. רבה בר בר חנה tells of enormously fat geese that seem to answer his question about עולם הבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These geese are linked to the reward of עולם הבא. By lifting parts of their bodies, they seem to answer 'yes' and show the portions that will be given. The next step explains why they are still waiting.

phrases.english: And Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:

phrases.aramaic: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה קָא אָזְלִינַן בְּמַדְבְּרָא,
phrases.english: Once we were traveling in the desert,
and we saw these geese
whose wings drooped because they were so fat,
and streams of oil flowed from beneath them.
I said to them:

phrases.aramaic: אִית לַן בְּגַוַּיְיכוּ חֻלָקָא לְעָלְמָא דְאָתֵי?
phrases.english: Do we have a portion of you in the World-to-Come?
One raised a wing,
and one raised a leg.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה קָא אָזְלִינַן בְּמַדְבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from sea stories to a desert story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The fat geese in the desert are reserved for ישראל in עולם הבא.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: ישראל will answer for the geese
steps.stepSummary: When רבה בר בר חנה reported this to רבי אלעזר, he said ישראל will one day be held accountable for these geese.
steps.simpleTranslation: When I came before רבי אלעזר, he said to me: ישראל will in the future be held accountable for them.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר explains the meaning of the geese story. ישראל will have to answer for keeping the geese waiting in their suffering.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The geese keep growing fatter while they wait to be given as reward. Because the reward is delayed, the delay is counted against ישראל. A wonder story becomes a message about responsibility.

keyTerms.meaning: To give an accounting, to be held responsible

steps.whatToRemember: The geese story ends with a lesson: רבי אלעזר says ישראל are responsible for how long the geese must wait for the promised reward.

phrases.english: When I came before Rabbi Elazar,
he said to me:

phrases.aramaic: עֲתִידִין יִשְׂרָאֵל לִיתֵּן עֲלֵיהֶן אֶת הַדִּין.
phrases.english: The Jewish people will in the future be held accountable for them.
phrases.notes: The geese are kept waiting and growing fatter until ישראל earn their reward, so the delay is counted against ישראל.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתַאי לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר, אָמַר לִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Interprets the meaning of the geese story in step 13.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: ישראל will be held accountable for the suffering of the waiting geese.

steps.title: A memory hook for the guide stories
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא gives a short סימן, a memory hook, for the stories about the Arab guide that are coming next.
steps.simpleTranslation: Memory hook: 'Like the dust; of the תכלת; a scorpion stung it; his basket.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pauses to give a short list of key words that help you remember the next group of stories. This line sets up what comes next. It is not a story by itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each word hints at one of the coming stories about the Arab guide. The first word, 'dust', points to the very next story, where the guide smells dust. A סימן like this helped people who learned by heart keep the stories in the right order.

keyTerms.meaning: A memory hook: a few key words that help you remember a series of teachings

steps.confusionAlert: This line is not part of any story. It is only a list of hint words for remembering the stories that follow.

phrases.english: (Memory hook: Like the dust; of the sky-blue;
phrases.notes: Each word in this memory hook points to one of the guide stories coming up. Some versions have these words in round brackets and some don't.

phrases.english: the scorpion stung it; his basket.)

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new group of רבה בר בר חנה stories after the geese story in Step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A memory hook listing the coming stories about the Arab guide.

steps.title: The guide who could smell the way
steps.stepSummary: An Arab guide could tell roads and the distance to water by smelling dust. רבה בר בר חנה tested him by switching the dust and could not fool him.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר בר חנה said: Once we were traveling in the desert, and an Arab joined us. He would take dust, smell it, and say, 'This road goes to such-and-such a place, and that road goes to such-and-such a place.' We asked him, 'How far are we from water?' He said, 'Give me dust.' We gave it to him, and he said, 'Eight פרסאות.' Later we gave him dust again, and he said we were three פרסאות away. I switched the dust to test him, but I could not fool him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה בר בר חנה tells about a desert guide who read the land just by smelling dust. When he tried to trick the guide with different dust, it did not work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story has three parts. First, the guide names roads by smell. Next, he measures the distance to water, and his answer changes correctly as they travel, from eight פרסאות to three. Last, a hidden test proves he truly knew the land and was not guessing. This sets him up as a trustworthy witness for the amazing things he shows next.

keyTerms.meaning: An Arab, a desert traveler or merchant
פרסאות, a long unit of distance (a few miles each)
I switched or turned it over

steps.whyThisMatters: Showing that the guide could not be fooled makes the reader trust him in the stories that follow, where he shows things from the time of the מדבר.

phrases.english: And Rabba bar bar Ḥana said:

phrases.aramaic: זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה קָא אָזְלִינַן בְּמַדְבְּרָא,
phrases.english: Once we were traveling in the desert,
and a certain Arab joined us
who would take dust and smell it,
and say: This is the road to such-and-such a place,
and that is the road to such-and-such a place.
We said to him: How far are we from water?
And he said to us: Give me dust.

phrases.aramaic: יָהֲבִינַן לֵיהּ, וְאָמַר לַן: תַּמְנֵי פַּרְסֵי.
phrases.english: We gave it to him, and he said to us: Eight parasangs.
We did it again and gave him dust,
and he said to us that we were three parasangs away.
I switched it on him, but I could not fool him.
phrases.notes: He secretly swapped in dust from a different place to test the guide, but the guide was not tricked.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר בַּר חָנָה זִימְנָא חֲדָא הֲוָה קָא אָזְלִינַן בְּמַדְבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: This is the first story named in the memory hook of Step 15 ('dust').
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The Arab guide could find roads and the distance to water by smelling dust, and could not be fooled.

steps.title: The guide shows the dead of the wilderness
steps.stepSummary: The guide offers to show רבה בר בר חנה the מתי מדבר. He goes and sees them, and they look like people who are drunk.
steps.simpleTranslation: The guide said to me: 'Come, I will show you the מתי מדבר.' I went and saw them, and they looked like people who were drunk,
steps.whatsHappening: A new story begins: the guide takes רבה בר בר חנה to see the generation of ישראל that died in the wilderness. The description of what they looked like starts here and continues after this text ends.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מתי מדבר are the people who left מצרים and died in the desert during the forty years. רבה בר בר חנה says they looked like people who were drunk. The sentence is not finished here, so this step sets up the details of their appearance that come next.

keyTerms.meaning: The dead of the wilderness: the generation that left מצרים and died in the desert

steps.confusionAlert: Do not stop here. The sentence ends with a comma and continues after this text with more details about how they looked.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לִי: תָּא אַחֲוֵי לָךְ מֵתֵי מִדְבָּר.
phrases.english: He said to me: Come, I will show you the dead of the wilderness.
phrases.notes: 'He' is the same Arab guide from the previous story.

phrases.english: I went and saw them,
and they looked like people who are drunk,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לִי תָּא אַחֲוֵי לָךְ מֵתֵי מִדְבָּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The same trustworthy guide from Step 16 now leads רבה בר בר חנה to a new sight.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The guide shows the מתי מדבר, who looked like drunk people.
